title: Repeat-Until Loop
subtitle: Master the post-test loop: at-least-once execution, exit-on-TRUE polarity, trace counting & infinite-loop traps

readingSections.title: What Is a Repeat-Until Loop?
readingSections.quickSummary: A REPEAT-UNTIL loop runs its body FIRST and tests the exit condition AFTER — so the body always executes at least once.
content: A REPEAT-UNTIL loop repeats a block of instructions UNTIL a condition becomes TRUE. Unlike the WHILE loop you already know, the condition sits at the BOTTOM of the loop: the body executes first, and only then is the test made.

This is called post-test (or exit-controlled) execution. Because the test happens after the body, the body is guaranteed to run at least once — even if the condition is already TRUE when the loop starts.
Placement exams love this loop because it breaks the habit built by WHILE questions: candidates assume the body can be skipped. In a REPEAT-UNTIL question it never can.

subsections.title: The shape of a REPEAT-UNTIL loop
subsections.content:
REPEAT
  PRINT n
  n = n + 1
UNTIL n > 3

REPEAT opens the block and UNTIL closes it with the test. There is no separate ENDWHILE-style closer: the condition itself ends the construct. Everything between REPEAT and UNTIL is the body, executed top to bottom on every pass.

subsections.title: Body first, test second
subsections.content: Trace order per pass: (1) run every statement of the body, (2) evaluate the UNTIL condition, (3) if FALSE go back to REPEAT, if TRUE fall through past UNTIL. A failing test still costs one full pass — that is exactly why x = 100 with UNTIL x > 50 still prints 100 once before stopping.

subsections.title: Same idea, different names
subsections.content: Cambridge/AQA pseudocode says REPEAT ... UNTIL. OCR writes do ... until. Pascal calls it repeat...until. C, C++ and Java have do-while — identical at-least-once behaviour, but the polarity is inverted: do-while CONTINUES while its condition is TRUE, whereas REPEAT-UNTIL continues while its condition is FALSE. Python has no post-test loop at all. Exam boards differ only in spelling; the logic is universal.

subsections.title: The three working parts
subsections.content: Every correct REPEAT-UNTIL has: an ACTION (the body), an UPDATE (a statement that moves some variable toward the exit condition), and a TEST (the UNTIL condition). Exams remove or break one of these to create wrong answers — most often they delete the UPDATE, producing an infinite loop.

quickRevision: Post-test = body runs BEFORE the check = minimum 1 pass, always.
Loop CONTINUES while the UNTIL condition is FALSE; exits the moment it turns TRUE.
do-while (C) = REPEAT-UNTIL with the condition negated.
No update statement toward the exit condition means an infinite loop.
tricks: Write 'min passes = 1' at the top of your scratch work before touching any REPEAT question — it kills the zero-pass trap instantly.
Cover the UNTIL line with your finger while tracing the first pass; it physically reminds you the test comes last.
If two options differ only by whether the first value prints, pick the one that prints it — post-test always pays for one pass.
REPEAT-UNTIL(C) equals DO-WHILE(NOT C). Convert mentally before comparing options that mix the two spellings.
patterns: 'How many times will the loop execute?' — count passes, remember pass 1 is free of any test.
'What will be the output?' — trace pass-by-pass; stop writing right after a TRUE test.
'Which loop should be used…' with words like 'at least once', 'prompt', 'menu', 'validate' — answer REPEAT-UNTIL / do-while.
'What happens when this code is executed?' where no variable ever changes — answer: infinite loop.

pyqPatterns.question: Which of the following is NOT a loop available in C? (for / while / do-while / repeat-until)
pyqPatterns.approach: C ships exactly three loops: for, while, do-while. repeat-until is Pascal/Cambridge-pseudocode vocabulary, so option D wins.

pyqPatterns.question: Which loop executes at least once even if the starting condition is false?
pyqPatterns.approach: Only the post-test family qualifies: do-while (and its twin REPEAT-UNTIL). Pre-test loops (for, while) can run zero times.

pyqPatterns.question: In the pseudocode below, what does REPEAT X = X + 1 UNTIL X >= 10 represent? (while loop / for loop / do-while / none)
pyqPatterns.approach: Test after body, exit on true — that is do-while behaviour with a negated condition.

readingSections.companyNote: Capgemini's pseudo-code round (about 20 questions in 20 minutes, elimination round), TCS NQT programming logic, Accenture pseudo-code quiz and the Infosys section all include 1-3 post-test loop questions per slot. They are among the fastest marks once the at-least-once reflex is trained.

readingSections.title: Exit-on-TRUE: The Inverted Condition Rule
readingSections.quickSummary: WHILE loops on TRUE; REPEAT-UNTIL loops on FALSE. Converting between them requires negating the condition — De Morgan included.
content: A WHILE loop keeps running while its condition stays TRUE and quits when it turns FALSE. A REPEAT-UNTIL loop does the exact opposite: it keeps running while its condition stays FALSE and quits the moment it turns TRUE.

This polarity flip is the number-one source of wrong answers in mixed-loop papers. Candidates read UNTIL n > 5 but keep tracing as if it were WHILE n > 5 — and continue looping when they should have stopped (or vice versa).
The fix is one mechanical rule: UNTIL(C) is equivalent to WHILE(NOT C). Before comparing options, translate every UNTIL into its WHILE twin using negation.

subsections.title: Negating conditions correctly
subsections.content: NOT(x > 5) is x <= 5 (note the equality moving across!). NOT(n = 0) is n <> 0. For compound tests use De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) becomes (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT(A OR B) becomes (NOT A) AND (NOT B). The AND/OR swap is the part everyone forgets under time pressure.

subsections.title: Worked conversion
subsections.content:
WHILE i <= 5 { PRINT i; i = i + 1 }
is the same loop as
i = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 5

Negating i <= 5 gives i > 5. Both print 1 2 3 4 5 — provided the starting value satisfies the WHILE condition. If the start FAILS the WHILE condition, the versions differ: WHILE prints nothing, REPEAT-UNTIL still runs once.

subsections.title: When conversion breaks down
subsections.content: WHILE and REPEAT-UNTIL are interchangeable only when the entry state makes the WHILE condition TRUE. If the WHILE would skip entirely, the REPEAT-UNTIL twin performs exactly one extra pass. Exam questions exploit precisely this boundary case — watch for initial values that violate the condition.

subsections.title: Compound exit conditions
subsections.content: UNTIL (mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100) keeps prompting until the mark lands inside 0..100. Its WHILE twin is WHILE (mark < 0 OR mark > 100). Range checks like this dominate input-validation PYQs: negate each side, flip AND to OR, flip every relational operator (> becomes <=, = becomes <>).

quickRevision: UNTIL(C) = WHILE(NOT C). Always convert before comparing loops.
Negate relations by flipping the operator AND sliding equality: > -> <=, >= -> <, = -> <>.
De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) = NOT(A) OR NOT(B); NOT(A OR B) = NOT(A) AND NOT(B).
Identical output only when the initial data satisfies the WHILE condition; otherwise REPEAT adds one pass.
tricks: Draw a tiny two-column table: 'continue?' vs 'stop?' and fill which polarity each keyword wants — takes ten seconds, saves the whole question.
For compound conditions, negate piece by piece on paper instead of trusting instinct: operator flips, AND<->OR swap.
Any option pair differing only by '<=' vs '<' is testing the equality slide; recheck which side the equality landed after negation.
Spot-check your conversion by plugging the boundary value into both versions; both must agree there.
patterns: Two answer choices that are De Morgan twins — the exam wants the properly swapped one.
WHILE-to-REPEAT rewrite questions: negate the condition, keep the body identical, move the test below.
'Equivalent loop' MCQs where one distractor forgets the AND->OR flip.
Boundary-value traps: does UNTIL x >= 10 stop AT 10 or AFTER? At 10 — the test fires immediately when x hits 10.

pyqPatterns.question: Set i = 3; do { print i+3; i = i - 1 } while(i < 0) — how many values are printed?
pyqPatterns.approach: do-while is post-test: the body runs once unconditionally (prints 6), THEN the test 2 < 0 fails. But wait — the test failing sends it BACK: 5, 4, 3 print too, exiting only at i = -1. Output 6 5 4 3. Polarity decides everything here.

pyqPatterns.source: AP CSP / Khan Academy conversion pattern
pyqPatterns.question: Rewrite WHILE (i <= 10) as REPEAT UNTIL (?).
pyqPatterns.approach: Negate: UNTIL i > 10 (equivalently i >= 11). Khan Academy teaches exactly this inversion recipe.

pyqPatterns.question: Complete REPEAT INPUT Mark UNTIL (?) so prompting repeats until a mark in 0..100 arrives.
pyqPatterns.approach: Continue while OUTSIDE the range: UNTIL Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100.

readingSections.companyNote: Infosys and Accenture frequently present do-while snippets whose condition polarity differs from a WHILE version shown alongside; Capgemini mixes bitwise traces with one polarity-flip trap. Mastering NOT-negation converts those into routine marks.

readingSections.title: Tracing Post-Test Loops & Counting Passes
readingSections.quickSummary: Build a pass-table: one row per pass, body first, test result last. Pass counts follow short closed formulas.
content: Tracing a REPEAT-UNTIL loop is the WHILE trace with the columns reordered: body actions happen in row k, then the test result closes row k. The loop ends in the row where the test first reads TRUE — that row IS counted as a pass.
Never merge rows mentally. One pass = one row = one set of variable updates. Most wrong options in output questions are simply off-by-one-row errors.
Pass counting also follows formulas you can use instead of tabulating when time is tight.

subsections.title: The pass-table method
subsections.content:
Columns: PASS | variables after body | UNTIL test | verdict.
Example — x = 2; REPEAT x = x * 2 UNTIL x > 30:
PASS 1: x = 4, 4 > 30 FALSE -> repeat
PASS 2: x = 8, FALSE
PASS 3: x = 16, FALSE
PASS 4: x = 32, TRUE -> exit. Answer: x = 32, four passes.

subsections.title: Counting formula for growing counters
subsections.content:
For REPEAT v = v + s UNTIL v >= T with start a and step s > 0: passes = ceil((T - a) / s).
Example: start 1, step 3, UNTIL v >= 20 -> ceil((20-1)/3) = ceil(6.33) = 7 passes (values 4,7,10,13,16,19,22).

subsections.title: Strict inequality variant
subsections.content:
For UNTIL v > B (strictly greater): passes = floor((B - a) / s) + 1.
Example: start 1, step 2, UNTIL v > 9 -> floor(8/2)+1 = 5 passes (values 3,5,7,9,11 — note 9 itself is not enough, 11 exits).

subsections.title: Shrinking and multiplicative patterns
subsections.content: Halving (v = v DIV 2): count how many halvings cross the threshold — 64 to UNTIL v <= 4 needs 32,16,8,4 = 4 passes. Doubling (v = v * 2): count doublings — 3 to UNTIL v >= 48 needs 6,12,24,48 = 4 passes. Countdowns mirror growth formulas with negative steps.

subsections.title: Final-value shortcut
subsections.content: After computing the pass count k, the final value is a + k*s (linear case). The printed sequence stops at the value produced IN the exiting pass; the next would-be value never appears. Questions asking 'what is printed LAST' want the entering-exit value, not the overshoot beyond it.

quickRevision: One row per pass; body updates first, test verdict last; the TRUE row still counts.
Growing counter, exit at v >= T: ceil((T-a)/s) passes.
Strict exit v > B: floor((B-a)/s)+1 passes.
Final linear value = a + k*s; last PRINTED value is the one made during the exiting pass.
tricks: List ONLY the control variable's after-body values in a single line (4, 8, 16, 32) and strike through the first one that satisfies UNTIL — fastest reliable count.
For step-1 loops from a upward to exit at B: passes = B - a when the test is v = B or v >= B.
Doubling/halving questions are log2 questions: count exponent hops, don't divide repeatedly on paper.
If asked 'how many times is X printed', put a tick in the pass-table row only when the print statement actually ran that pass.
patterns: 'How many times does the loop execute?' with clean arithmetic start/step/target — apply the formula, verify with a 2-row spot check.
'Print the output' where the body prints before updating — sequence ends with the exiting pass's value.
'What is the final value of the counter?' — always one step PAST the last printed value when update follows print.
Nested FOR-outside/REPEAT-inside: multiply inner passes by outer iterations, then add any leftover statements.

pyqPatterns.question: Integer i; Set i = 3; REPEAT PRINT i + 3; i = i - 1 UNTIL i = 0 — predict the output.
pyqPatterns.approach: Post-test trace: pass 1 prints 6 (i=2), pass 2 prints 5 (i=1), pass 3 prints 4 (i=0) -> exit. Output 6 5 4.

pyqPatterns.question: x = 40; REPEAT x = x DIV 2 UNTIL x < 5 — how many iterations?
pyqPatterns.approach: 20, 10, 5, 2 — the fourth halving crosses below 5, so 4 iterations, final x = 2.

pyqPatterns.question: n = 29; REPEAT s = s + n MOD 10; n = n DIV 10 UNTIL n = 0 — what is s?
pyqPatterns.approach: Digit-sum pipeline: picks 9 then 2 -> s = 11. Same skeleton as WHILE digit questions; only the test position changed.

readingSections.companyNote: Nearly every service-company paper contains one straight trace (like the Capgemini i=3 item) and one pass-count item. With the formula + spot-check combo both take under thirty seconds each.

readingSections.title: Validation, Menus & Sentinel Loops
readingSections.quickSummary: Prompt-at-least-once tasks (input validation, menus, passwords) are the natural home of REPEAT-UNTIL — and a fixed set of exam stems.
content: Whenever a program must ASK FIRST and CHECK AFTER — password prompts, menu redisplay, range-checked marks — the post-test loop is the textbook fit. The prompt itself is the body; the validity test is the UNTIL line.
Exams test this as concept MCQs ('which loop guarantees the menu shows at least once?') and as numeric traces ('how many prompts/read operations happened?'). Both reduce to counting passes.
Sentinel-controlled variants read values until a special terminator (-1, 0, empty string) appears. The sentinel value is consumed by READ and typically excluded from sums via IF guards.

subsections.title: Input-validation template
subsections.content:
REPEAT
  OUTPUT "Enter marks (0..100): "
  INPUT mark
UNTIL mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100
OUTPUT "Accepted"

The loop re-prompts while the input is INVALID; the moment a valid value arrives the condition goes TRUE and flow leaves the loop with 'mark' holding the accepted value.

subsections.title: Menu template
subsections.content:
REPEAT
  DISPLAY menu
  INPUT choice
  IF choice = 1 THEN ... ELSE IF choice = 2 THEN ...
UNTIL choice = exitValue

Menus must render at least once by definition, so a WHILE version needs artificial priming; REPEAT-UNTIL needs none. Expect 'why is REPEAT better here?' as a theory question.

subsections.title: Counting prompts in trace form
subsections.content: Given inputs arriving in order, each pass consumes exactly one INPUT. Prompts = passes. Example: validation above fed 150 then 55 -> pass 1 rejects 150, pass 2 accepts 55 -> exactly 2 prompts. This 'count the reads' stem appears in Wipro and Cocubes papers.

subsections.title: Sentinel template
subsections.content:
count = 0
REPEAT
  READ num
  count = count + 1
  IF num <> -1 THEN sum = sum + num
UNTIL num = -1

Note the guard: the sentinel enters the READ (that is how the test sees it) but must be kept out of accumulation. Wrong answers usually either skip the sentinel's read or include it in the sum.

quickRevision: Ask-first tasks (prompt/menu/password) -> REPEAT-UNTIL; may-skip tasks -> WHILE.
Prompts = reads = passes; count them row by row.
Range check exits when INSIDE the range; sentinel loop exits when the sentinel is read.
Guard accumulators against the sentinel with IF num <> sentinel.
tricks: In 'how many prompts' questions, just tally inputs consumed — no arithmetic needed.
Menu theory answer template: 'menu must display at least once; post-test avoids priming read'.
Sentinel questions: underline the sentinel first; anything compared to it is the exit row.
If a trace feeds more valid inputs than listed before a sentinel, suspect a misread — exams always list enough inputs to terminate.
patterns: 'Which construct is best for…' + words 'at least once / prompt / validate / menu' -> REPEAT-UNTIL.
'How many times is the user prompted?' given a fixed input list -> count list items until the accept/sentinel one.
Password attempts: passes = attempts allowed before success; success attempt still counts.
Sum-with-sentinel traces where the sentinel is -1 or 0 and must not enter the total.

pyqPatterns.question: REPEAT INPUT Colour UNTIL Colour = "red" — describe execution.
pyqPatterns.approach: Classic Save-My-Exams example: prompts at least once, repeats while the colour is wrong, exits when 'red' typed.

pyqPatterns.question: Inputs arrive 4, 9, -1. count = 0; REPEAT READ num; count = count + 1 UNTIL num = -1. What is count?
pyqPatterns.approach: Three reads including the sentinel: count = 3. The sentinel IS read — that is how the loop detects it.

pyqPatterns.question: Marks validation loop with tried inputs 150, 55 — how many prompts appear?

readingSections.companyNote: Theory stems ('best loop for menu/validation') show up in TCS NQT and Infosys sections; numeric prompt-count traces appear in Wipro and Cocubes papers. Both styles are formulaic — recognise the template, bank the mark.

readingSections.title: Infinite Loop Traps & the Exam Checklist
readingSections.quickSummary: Missing updates, parity skips and net-zero changes turn REPEAT-UNTIL into an endless loop — exams ask you to spot all three.
content: A REPEAT-UNTIL terminates only if the body eventually drives the UNTIL condition to TRUE. Three sabotage patterns appear constantly:

(1) MISSING UPDATE — the tested variable never changes inside the body, so the test answer is frozen. (2) PARITY/OVERSHTOOT SKIP — the update jumps OVER the target (stepping +2 through an even target, doubling through 100, decrementing by 3 through 0). (3) NET-ZERO CHANGE — the body cancels itself (x = x - 1 then x = x + 1), leaving the test value motionless.

All three produce the same verdict: the loop never ends. Options usually pair 'runs once' against 'runs forever' — the at-least-once rule guarantees at least the once, so 'runs once' is only right when the FIRST test already returns TRUE.

subsections.title: Trap 1 — missing update
subsections.content:
flag = FALSE
count = 0
REPEAT
  PRINT count
UNTIL flag = TRUE
flag is never touched inside the body -> test stays FALSE forever -> infinite loop printing count endlessly. Any snippet whose UNTIL variable appears nowhere in the body is automatically infinite.

subsections.title: Trap 2 — skipping the target
subsections.content:
x = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT x
  x = x + 2
UNTIL x = 8
x walks odd numbers 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 … and NEVER equals 8. Equality tests demand the step land exactly on the target; otherwise the loop oversteps forever. Safer authoring uses inequalities (UNTIL x >= 8), which exams sometimes offer as the 'fixed version' option.

subsections.title: Trap 3 — net-zero updates
subsections.content:
res = 5
REPEAT
  res = res - 1
  res = res + 1
UNTIL res = 0
Each pass restores res to 5; the test never sees 0 -> infinite. An Infosys do-while PYQ used exactly this decrement-increment alternation. Scan the body for self-cancelling pairs whenever 'infinite loop' is an option.

subsections.title: The 15-second exam checklist
subsections.content: Before answering ANY REPEAT-UNTIL question: (1) Which variable does UNTIL test? (2) Does the body change it? (3) Does the change move TOWARD satisfying the test without skipping it? (4) Trace pass 1 fully — remember it happens regardless. (5) Stop writing the instant the test reads TRUE. These five checks catch every published trap pattern.

quickRevision: Tested variable unchanged in body -> infinite.
Step skips the equality target (parity/magnitude mismatch) -> infinite.
-1 followed by +1 style cancellations -> infinite.
Even doomed loops run their first pass; 'executes at least once' remains true for infinite loops' first iteration.
tricks: Circle the UNTIL variable, then hunt for it in the body — absent means infinite, no tracing needed.
Equality target + non-unit step: check divisibility (target - start) mod step == 0; nonzero remainder predicts an infinite skip loop.
When 'infinite loop' and a numeric output are both offered, run the divisibility check BEFORE hand-tracing — it settles the choice in seconds.
Net-zero scan: pair up increments/decrements on the same variable; balanced pairs mean a frozen test.
patterns: Options containing 'will run infinitely' alongside concrete numbers — the setter planted one of the three sabotages.
Decrement-increment alternation bodies (Infosys favourite) — always infinite.
'Fixed version' questions: replacing = with >= (or adding the missing update) is the repair to select.
While-vs-repeat comparison where the initial value violates the condition: WHILE skips (zero passes), REPEAT still burns one pass.

pyqPatterns.question: Inside a do-while, res is decremented and incremented alternately — what happens on execution?
pyqPatterns.approach: Net-zero drift keeps the condition permanently satisfied -> code runs an infinite number of times.

pyqPatterns.question: A WHILE loop assigns (=) instead of compares inside its header condition — what happens?
pyqPatterns.approach: Assignment keeps yielding truthy -> infinite loop. Distinguish '=' misuse from genuine comparisons in loop headers.

pyqPatterns.question: x = 10; REPEAT x = x - 3 UNTIL x = 0 — what happens?
pyqPatterns.approach: Sequence 7, 4, 1, -2 … skips 0 forever -> infinite loop. Divisibility check (10-0) mod 3 != 0 flags it instantly.

readingSections.companyNote: Infinite-or-not MCQs appear in nearly every TCS NQT, Infosys and Cocubes slot because they are quick to grade and brutal to guess. The three named traps cover essentially every published instance — memorise them, don't rediscover them mid-exam.

formulas.title: Body-Before-Check Rule (Minimum One Pass)

formula.text: The body of a REPEAT-UNTIL loop executes at least ONCE, no matter what the UNTIL condition says.

formulas.whenToUse: Any question about how few times a post-test loop can run, or whether the first statement executes when the condition starts TRUE/false.
explanation: Control reaches REPEAT and falls straight INTO the body — no gate exists above it.
Only after the full body runs is the UNTIL condition evaluated for the first time.
TRUE -> leave the loop having spent exactly one pass; FALSE -> climb back and spend another.
Therefore the theoretical minimum is 1 pass (never 0), and even a condition already TRUE at entry costs one body execution.

example.prompt:
i = 100
REPEAT
  PRINT i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 50
steps: Ignore the condition initially — the body must run: PRINT 100.
First test ever made: is 101 > 50? TRUE -> exit.

formulas.memoryTip: Post-test = pay first, check later. The body ALWAYS pays one pass.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering 'nothing prints because 100 > 50 already' — that reasoning belongs to WHILE loops, not REPEAT-UNTIL.

formulas.title: Exit-on-TRUE Polarity & Negation Rule

formula.text: A REPEAT-UNTIL continues while C is FALSE and exits when C becomes TRUE. It equals a WHILE loop running on the negated condition.

formulas.whenToUse: Converting loops, comparing WHILE/do-while options, or deciding the exact stopping row of a trace.
explanation: WHILE(C): continue on TRUE, stop on FALSE. UNTIL(C): continue on FALSE, stop on TRUE — perfect opposites.
Negate relations by flipping the operator and sliding equality: > becomes <=, >= becomes <, = becomes <>.
Compound rules need De Morgan: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B); NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B) — operators AND/OR swap too.
Conversion is output-identical ONLY when the entry data satisfies the WHILE condition; otherwise the REPEAT version spends one extra pass.

example.prompt: Rewrite WHILE (i <= 5) { body } as a REPEAT-UNTIL.
steps: Keep the body identical and move the test below it.
Negate i <= 5: flip <= to >, giving i > 5.

formulas.memoryTip: UNTIL means 'run until it turns TRUE' — the condition describes the STOP state, not the run state.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing UNTIL i <= 5 for a WHILE i <= 5 twin — forgetting to negate keeps looping backwards.

formulas.title: Pass-Counting Formulas

formula.latex: k = \left\lceil \frac{T-a}{s} \right\rceil \quad(\text{UNTIL } v \geq T);\qquad k = \left\lfloor \frac{B-a}{s} \right\rfloor + 1 \quad(\text{UNTIL } v > B)
formula.text: Starting at a with additive step s: ceiling of the gap for '>=' exits, floor-plus-one for strict '>' exits.

formulas.whenToUse: 'How many times does the loop execute?' questions with linear counters — skip the table, compute directly.
explanation: After k passes a growing counter holds a + k*s; find the smallest k satisfying the exit test.
UNTIL v >= T: smallest k with a + k*s >= T is ceil((T-a)/s).
UNTIL v > B: smallest k with a + k*s > B is floor((B-a)/s) + 1 (equality on B is not enough).
Halving/doubling loops are logarithmic: count the multiplicative hops across the threshold instead of dividing repeatedly.
Always sanity-spot-check the last two values before trusting the formula under exam pressure.

example.prompt: x = 1; REPEAT x = x + 3 UNTIL x >= 20 — how many passes?
steps: Verify tail: after 6 passes x = 19 (< 20, keep going), after 7 passes x = 22 (>= 20, exit).

formulas.memoryTip: Ceiling for 'reaches', floor+one for 'crosses strictly beyond'.
formulas.commonMistake: Using floor((T-a)/s) alone — it can under-count by one when the gap divides evenly or when equality matters.

formulas.title: WHILE <-> REPEAT-UNTIL Conversion Kit

formula.text: Move the test below the body and negate it with De Morgan to convert in either direction.

formulas.whenToUse: Equivalence MCQs, rewriting questions, and any option set mixing WHILE and UNTIL spellings of the same logic.
explanation: Three-step recipe: copy the body unchanged; place the original condition BELOW the body after UNTIL; negate it fully.
Full negation = operator flip (+ equality slide) on each atom, AND<->OR swap between atoms.
Example atoms: n > 0 AND n <> 99 negates to n <= 0 OR n = 99.
The converted pair behaves identically only when the initial state satisfies the WHILE test; else the post-test twin adds exactly one pass.
C-language bridge: REPEAT B UNTIL(C) is literally do { B } while (!C);.

example.prompt: Convert REPEAT body UNTIL (a > 5 AND b < 3) into a WHILE continuation condition.
steps: Negation of the UNTIL condition gives the WHILE continue-condition.
De Morgan: NOT(a > 5 AND b < 3) = (a <= 5) OR (b >= 3).
So the twin is WHILE (a <= 5 OR b >= 3) { body }.

formulas.memoryTip: Flip every sign, swap AND/OR, and the equality always slides to the other side.
formulas.commonMistake: Negating atoms but keeping the connector (AND stays AND) — the classic De Morgan drop.

formulas.title: Accumulator Tracing Across Passes

formula.text: Running totals/products fold one contribution per pass; the answer is the state right after the exiting pass.

formulas.whenToUse: Output-prediction traces that sum, multiply, reverse digits, or build strings inside the loop.
explanation: Track accumulator(s) in dedicated columns; each pass appends exactly one contribution.
Digit pipelines (MOD/DIV pairs) contribute one digit per pass: sums add them, reversals shift-and-add (rev = rev*10 + d).
Product accumulators multiply — factorial skeletons hit p = p * i with i climbing by one.
String builders concatenate; length grows by the chunk size per pass.
Freeze all values immediately after the exiting pass's body — later contributions do not exist.

example.prompt:
num = 47; rev = 0
REPEAT
  d = num MOD 10
  rev = rev * 10 + d
  num = num DIV 10
UNTIL num = 0
PRINT rev
steps: Pass 1: d = 7, rev = 0*10 + 7 = 7, num = 4. Test 4 = 0 FALSE.
Pass 2: d = 4, rev = 7*10 + 4 = 74, num = 0. Test TRUE -> exit.
PRINT rev shows 74 — digits of 47 reversed.

formulas.memoryTip: Reverse-number = shift-left-then-add-digit, one digit per pass, stop when DIV starves num to zero.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the sentinel/final zero pass — once the test is TRUE no further body line runs.

formulas.title: Infinite-Loop Detector (3 Sabotage Checks)

formula.text: Untested-variable, target-skipping, or net-zero bodies make a REPEAT-UNTIL run forever.

formulas.whenToUse: Whenever 'infinite loop / runs forever' is among the options — screen before tracing.
explanation: CHECK 1 — presence: does the variable inside UNTIL(...) get assigned anywhere in the body? If not, the loop cannot end.
CHECK 2 — reachability: for equality exits, does (target - start) divide evenly by the step? A remainder means the walk skips the target forever (e.g., odds chasing 8).
CHECK 3 — net progress: cancel paired +k/-k edits on the tested variable; zero net movement freezes the test (the Infosys decrement-increment PYQ).
All three failures share one symptom: the UNTIL condition can never read TRUE.
Remember the guarantee cuts BOTH ways: even doomed loops execute their first pass before stalling.

example.prompt:
x = 10
REPEAT
  x = x - 3
UNTIL x = 0
steps: CHECK 2: (10 - 0) mod 3 = 1, remainder nonzero -> the countdown skips 0.

formulas.memoryTip: Updated? Reachable? Progressing? Any NO = infinite loop.
formulas.commonMistake: Declaring termination because 'it will eventually get there' — modular arithmetic says otherwise; trust the divisibility check.

post-test-first-pass.q:
x = 9
REPEAT
  PRINT x
UNTIL x > 100
What is printed?
s: Post-test: body runs before any check.
Pass 1 prints 9; test 9 > 100 is FALSE.
No update exists on x, so every later test also fails -> loop repeats forever.
post-test-first-pass.a: 9 printed once, then infinitely repeated (first line is always 9)

post-test-first-pass.q: Regardless of initial variable values, a REPEAT-UNTIL body executes at least ___ time(s).
s: The UNTIL test sits below the body.
Control enters the body unconditionally on the first visit.
Hence minimum one pass, even with the condition already TRUE.

post-test-first-pass.q: How many times per pass is the exit condition evaluated in a REPEAT-UNTIL loop?
s: Post-test loops make exactly one evaluation per pass, positioned after the body completes.
WHILE loops evaluate once per pass too, but BEFORE the body.

post-test-first-pass.q:
x = 0
REPEAT
  x = x + 1
UNTIL TRUE
PRINT x
s: Body runs first: x becomes 1.
Test TRUE fires immediately -> exit after one pass.
PRINT shows 1.

post-test-first-pass.q:
i = 20. How many lines does this print?
REPEAT
  PRINT i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 25
s: Prints happen for i = 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 (six values).
After printing 25, i becomes 26 and 26 > 25 stops the loop.

post-test-first-pass.q: A REPEAT-UNTIL whose condition is FALSE on entry and can never become TRUE will:
s: Entry state is irrelevant — one pass happens anyway.
With no path to TRUE, control returns to REPEAT endlessly.

post-test-first-pass.q: In flowchart language, a post-test loop is called:
s: The controlling test sits at the loop's exit point, hence exit-controlled.
Pre-test loops are entry-controlled; FOR is count-controlled.

post-test-first-pass.q:
REPEAT
  READ value
UNTIL valid(value)
The MINIMUM number of READ operations is:
s: READ belongs to the body, which executes at least once.
Even a valid first input still gets read once before the test accepts it.

post-test-first-pass.q:
x = 3
REPEAT
  x = x * 2
UNTIL x >= 12
PRINT x
s: Pass 1: x = 6; test 6 >= 12 FALSE.
Pass 2: x = 12; test TRUE -> exit.
PRINT shows 12.

post-test-first-pass.q: True or False: if the UNTIL condition is already TRUE when execution reaches REPEAT, the body still executes exactly once.
opts: Only when the body has one statement
s: There is no gate above the body.
One full pass runs, then the TRUE test releases control.

exit-on-true.q: A REPEAT-UNTIL loop keeps repeating as long as its UNTIL condition evaluates to ___.
s: UNTIL describes the STOP state: exit when TRUE.
So continuation requires the opposite — FALSE.

exit-on-true.q:
n = 1
REPEAT
  n = n + 1
UNTIL n = 5
How many passes?
s: n walks 2, 3, 4, 5 across four passes.
At n = 5 the equality test turns TRUE -> stop.

exit-on-true.q: Which WHILE continuation condition matches REPEAT ... UNTIL (x >= 10)?
s: UNTIL(x >= 10) means: continue while NOT(x >= 10).
Negating slides equality across: NOT(x >= 10) = x < 10.
So the twin is WHILE (x < 10).

exit-on-true.q: REPEAT ... UNTIL (NOT found) is equivalent to which do-while form?
s: do-while(C) continues while C holds.
UNTIL(NOT found) continues while found is TRUE.
So the twin is do body while(found).

exit-on-true.q:
x = 8
REPEAT
  x = x - 2
UNTIL x = 2
Number of passes:
s: Walk: 6 (F), 4 (F), 2 (TRUE).
Three passes total.

exit-on-true.q: Which condition makes the loop exit as soon as x turns negative?
s: Exit-on-negative is literally UNTIL x < 0.
Option D over-constrains to exactly -1 and skips other negatives.

exit-on-true.q:
count = 0
REPEAT
  count = count + 1
UNTIL count = 5
Final value of count:
s: Passes lift count 1..5.
At 5 the test exits; nothing pushes it further.

exit-on-true.q: score = 105 and the loop reads REPEAT body UNTIL score > 100. How many times does the BODY run?
s: Post-test guarantees one execution regardless of the entry state.
After that first pass, 105 > 100 exits immediately.

exit-on-true.q: Rewrite UNTIL (a = b) as a WHILE continuation condition.
s: Continue while the exit test fails.
NOT(a = b) is a <> b.

exit-on-true.q: Loop continues while 0 < x < 100. Its UNTIL exit condition is:
s: Exit when OUTSIDE the range: below-or-equal 0 or above-or-equal 100.
De Morgan on NOT(0<x AND x<100) gives x<=0 OR x>=100.

counter-iterations.q: x = 1; REPEAT x = x + 2 UNTIL x > 9 — how many passes?
s: Values after each pass: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
11 is the first strictly greater than 9 -> 5 passes.
Formula floor((9-1)/2)+1 = 5.

counter-iterations.q: v = 0; REPEAT v = v + 7 UNTIL v >= 35 — passes?
s: Tail check: 28 (F), 35 (T).

counter-iterations.q: n = 10; REPEAT n = n - 3 UNTIL n < 0 — passes?
s: Sequence: 7, 4, 1, -2.
-2 < 0 exits -> 4 passes.

counter-iterations.q: m = 64; REPEAT m = m DIV 2 UNTIL m <= 4 — passes?
s: Halving chain: 32, 16, 8, 4.
4 <= 4 exits -> 4 passes.

counter-iterations.q: t = 3; REPEAT t = t * 2 UNTIL t >= 48 — passes?
s: 48 >= 48 exits -> 4 passes.

counter-iterations.q: u = 100; REPEAT u = u - 25 UNTIL u = 0 — passes?
s: Equality lands exactly on the fourth pass.

counter-iterations.q: For start a, step s > 0, exit UNTIL v >= T, the pass count equals:
s: Smallest k with a + k*s >= T is the ceiling of the gap ratio.

counter-iterations.q: w = 5; REPEAT w = w + 5 UNTIL w > 20 — passes?
s: Strict exit needs w beyond 20: values 10, 15, 20, 25.
25 crosses -> 4 passes; floor((20-5)/5)+1 = 4.

counter-iterations.q: p = 1; REPEAT p = p * 2 UNTIL p > 100 — passes?
s: 128 first exceeds 100 -> 7 passes.

counter-iterations.q: z = 90; REPEAT z = z - 10 UNTIL z < 20 — passes?
s: 80,70,60,50,40,30,20 all fail (< 20 false at 20), then 10 succeeds.
Eight passes total.
Move the test below and negate.

while-conversion.q: REPEAT body UNTIL (x = 0) equals which WHILE loop?
s: Continuation = negation of exit test.
Negate both atoms: n > 0 -> n <= 0; n <> 99 -> n = 99.
AND flips to OR under De Morgan.

while-conversion.q: UNTIL (a >= 5 AND b >= 5) as a WHILE continuation is:
s: Flip relations sliding equality: a >= 5 -> a < 5; b >= 5 -> b < 5.
Swap AND to OR.

while-conversion.q: Both versions print the same output ONLY WHEN:
opts: the initial data satisfies the WHILE condition
s: If WHILE would skip at entry, REPEAT-UNTIL still spends one pass.
Identical behaviour therefore requires an initially-true WHILE test.
while-conversion.a: Initial data satisfies the WHILE condition

while-conversion.q: An infinite WHILE(TRUE){B} matches which REPEAT form?
s: Endless continuation needs an exit test that never fires.
UNTIL FALSE never exits — same infinite behaviour.

opts: the iteration count and outputs (given a satisfiable entry)
s: Conversion is semantic-preserving apart from the zero-pass boundary case.
while-conversion.a: Iteration count and outputs (when entry satisfies the WHILE test)

s: Double negation: NOT(NOT flag) = flag.
Continue while flag holds TRUE.

opts: UNTIL x MOD 2 = 1 only when x odd
s: Negate the parity test: NOT(even) = odd = x MOD 2 <> 0.

while-conversion.q: The most common conversion error seen in exam distractors is:
opts: negating atoms but not swapping AND/OR
s: De Morgan drop keeps AND where OR belongs, silently widening/narrowing the exit set.
while-conversion.a: Skipping the AND/OR swap during negation

output-accumulation.q:
s = 0, i = 1
REPEAT
  s = s + i
  i = i + 2
UNTIL i > 7
PRINT s

p = 2, i = 3
REPEAT
  p = p * i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 5
PRINT p
s: i reaches 6 -> exit.

output-accumulation.q:
num = 123, rev = 0
REPEAT
  d = num MOD 10
  rev = rev*10 + d
  num = num DIV 10
UNTIL num = 0
PRINT rev
s: Digits pulled: 3, then 2, then 1.
rev builds 3 -> 32 -> 321.

output-accumulation.q:
n = 249, dp = 1
REPEAT
  dp = dp * (n MOD 10)
  n = n DIV 10
UNTIL n = 0
PRINT dp
s: Digit product: 9 * 4 * 2.

output-accumulation.q:
k = 4
REPEAT
  PRINT k
  k = k - 1
UNTIL k = 0
s: Prints 4, 3, 2, 1.
After printing 1, k becomes 0 and equality exits — 0 itself is never printed.

output-accumulation.q:
s = 0, i = 1
REPEAT
  s = s + i * i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 3
PRINT s, i
s: i ends at 4 (the failing-test value).

output-accumulation.q:
a = 0, b = 1
REPEAT
  a = a + b
  b = a * 2
UNTIL b > 8
PRINT a, b
s: Sequential updates: pass1 a=1,b=2; pass2 a=3,b=6; pass3 a=9,b=18.
18 > 8 exits.

output-accumulation.q:
Inputs arrive: 5, 2, 9, -1.
m = 0
REPEAT
  READ x
  IF x > m THEN m = x
UNTIL x = -1
PRINT m
s: Guard keeps the sentinel out: m tracks max(5,2,9).
Sentinel -1 read -> exit; PRINT 9.

output-accumulation.q:
sum = 0, c = 0, v = 2
REPEAT
  sum = sum + v
  c = c + 1
  v = v + 2
UNTIL v > 6
PRINT sum / c
s: Adds 2, 4, 6 with counts 1, 2, 3.
sum = 12, c = 3 -> average 4.

output-accumulation.q:
t = "", c = 0
REPEAT
  t = t + "*"
  c = c + 1
UNTIL c = 4
PRINT LENGTH(t)
s: One star per pass, four passes.
Length 4.

infinite-loop-check.q:
x = 5
REPEAT
  x = x + 1
UNTIL x = 5
Verdict?
s: Body moves x UP to 6 before any test.
Counting upward from 6 never revisits 5 -> endless.

infinite-loop-check.q:
flag = FALSE
count = 0
REPEAT
  PRINT count
UNTIL flag = TRUE
Why does this loop forever?
opts: flag is never updated inside the body
s: The tested variable appears nowhere in the body — sabotage check 1 fails.
infinite-loop-check.a: flag is never changed inside the loop

infinite-loop-check.q:
x = 10
REPEAT
  x = x - 2
UNTIL x = 5
Verdict?
s: Walk: 8, 6, 4, 2, 0, -2 … never lands on 5.
Divisibility check: (10 - 5) mod 2 = 1, nonzero -> equality target unreachable.

infinite-loop-check.q:
res = 5
REPEAT
  res = res - 1
  res = res + 1
UNTIL res = 0
Verdict?
s: Paired -1/+1 cancel each pass (Infosys PYQ skeleton).
Test sees a frozen 5 forever.

infinite-loop-check.q:
y = 10
REPEAT
  y = y - 3
UNTIL y = 0
Verdict?
s: (10-0) mod 3 = 1 -> target skipped forever.

infinite-loop-check.q: Which single repair terminates  q = 1; REPEAT q = q * 2 UNTIL q = 100 ?
s: Powers of two never equal 100.
An inequality (>=) catches the crossing instead of the landing.

infinite-loop-check.q:
g = 9
REPEAT
  g = g - 1
  g = g + 1
UNTIL g = 0
This mirrors which published PYQ pattern?
s: Net-zero drift on the tested variable — the documented Infosys trap.

opts: m=64; REPEAT m=m DIV 2 UNTIL m<=4
s: Option A skips even target; C never sets flag; D assigns r to itself.
Only B's inequality halving reaches 4 <= 4.
infinite-loop-check.a: m = 64; REPEAT m = m DIV 2 UNTIL m <= 4

infinite-loop-check.q:
w = 1
REPEAT
  w = w * 2
UNTIL w = 100
Verdict?
s: Doubling visits 2,4,8,…,64,128 — 100 lies off the lattice.
Equality test never satisfied.

infinite-loop-check.q:
e = 1
REPEAT
  e = e + 3
UNTIL e >= 10
Terminates? Final e?
s: Walk the counter: 4, 7, 10.
At e = 10 the test 10 >= 10 fires TRUE -> exit; final value 10, three passes.

mcqs.q: In a REPEAT-UNTIL loop, what is the MINIMUM number of times the body can execute?
exp: The UNTIL test sits below the body.
Control enters the body before any test is made.
So one pass always happens — zero is impossible.
mcqs.shortcut: Post-test loop = minimum 1 pass. Pre-test (WHILE/FOR) = minimum 0.

mcqs.q: When is the exit condition checked in a REPEAT-UNTIL construct?
opts: Only once when the program starts
exp: REPEAT-UNTIL is a post-test (exit-controlled) loop.
The body executes first; only then is the UNTIL condition evaluated.
mcqs.pattern: 'When is the condition tested?' -> post-test means AFTER the body, every pass.

mcqs.q: A REPEAT-UNTIL loop keeps repeating as long as its UNTIL condition evaluates to ___.
exp: UNTIL names the STOP state: exit when TRUE.
Continuation therefore requires FALSE.
mcqs.shortcut: WHILE runs on TRUE; UNTIL runs on FALSE. Perfect mirrors.

mcqs.q:
x = 5
REPEAT
  x = x + 1
UNTIL x > 5
PRINT x
What is printed?
exp: Pass 1: body lifts x to 6.
Test: 6 > 5 TRUE -> exit after one pass.
PRINT shows 6.

mcqs.q: Which loop is guaranteed to run AT LEAST once even if its condition is false at the start?
exp: WHILE and FOR check first and can skip entirely.
REPEAT-UNTIL checks last, so the body always executes once.

mcqs.q:
n = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT n
  n = n + 1
UNTIL n = 4
What does this print?
exp: Prints happen for n = 1, 2, 3.
After printing 3, n becomes 4 and the equality test exits — 4 itself is never printed.
mcqs.shortcut: The value that satisfies an equality UNTIL is reached but NOT printed if print precedes update.

mcqs.q:
How many times does the body execute?
x = 10
REPEAT
  x = x + 5
UNTIL x > 20
exp: After-body values: 15, 20, 25.
25 is the first strictly greater than 20 -> 3 passes.

mcqs.q:
i = 100
REPEAT
  PRINT i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 50
What happens?
exp: Entry state cannot block a post-test body.
One pass prints 100; then 101 > 50 exits immediately.
mcqs.pattern: Condition already satisfied at entry + REPEAT-UNTIL = exactly ONE pass.

mcqs.q: Where is the stopping condition written in a REPEAT-UNTIL construct?
opts: At the top next to REPEAT
exp: REPEAT opens the body; UNTIL closes it carrying the condition.
Its physical position mirrors WHEN it runs — last.

mcqs.q: C's do-while continues while its condition is TRUE. A Pascal-style REPEAT-UNTIL stops when its condition becomes ___.
exp: Both are post-test loops differing only in polarity.
do-while(C) = REPEAT UNTIL(NOT C).
mcqs.source: Standard TCS NQT / Infosys comparison stem

mcqs.q:
s = 0, i = 2
REPEAT
  s = s + i
  i = i + 2
UNTIL i > 6
PRINT s
exp: Contributions: +2 (i=4), +4 (i=6), +6 (i=8).

mcqs.q: A post-test loop is also called:
exp: The controlling test sits at the exit point of the loop.
Pre-test loops are entry-controlled.

mcqs.q:
n = 3
REPEAT
  PRINT n
  n = n - 1
UNTIL n = 0
Output?
exp: Prints 3, 2, 1 across three passes.
n reaches 0 only after printing 1; equality then ends the loop.

mcqs.q: Which task fits a REPEAT-UNTIL loop BEST?
opts: Asking for a password until correct (must prompt at least once)
Checking whether a file is empty before reading it
Printing squares of the first five numbers
exp: Prompt-at-least-once tasks are the natural post-test home.
Fixed-count tasks suit FOR; may-skip tasks suit WHILE.

mcqs.q:
a = 1
REPEAT
  a = a * 2
UNTIL a >= 8
PRINT a
exp: Doubling chain: 2, 4, 8.
8 >= 8 fires TRUE -> exit; three passes.

mcqs.q: Regardless of starting values, the body of a do-while / REPEAT-UNTIL loop executes at least ___ time(s).
exp: TCS NQT phrasing of the classic guarantee question.
Test-after loops pay for one pass unconditionally.

mcqs.q:
k = 0
REPEAT
  k = k + 3
UNTIL k >= 9
PRINT k
exp: Values: 3, 6, 9.
9 >= 9 exits on the third pass.

mcqs.q: Convert WHILE x < 10 into an equivalent UNTIL condition.
exp: Negation slides the equality across: NOT(x < 10) = x >= 10.
UNTIL(x >= 10) exits exactly where WHILE(x < 10) would stop looping.
mcqs.shortcut: Flip the operator AND move '=' to the other side.

mcqs.q:
x = 7
REPEAT
  PRINT x MOD 2
  x = x DIV 2
UNTIL x = 0
Output?
exp: Passes: 7->(print 1)->3; 3->(print 1)->1; 1->(print 1)->0.
Three odd halvings print 1 three times; x = 0 exits.
mcqs.pattern: MOD/DIV pipeline prints the binary digits of 7 from least significant end.

mcqs.q: True or False: if the UNTIL condition is TRUE before the loop starts, the body still executes exactly once.
opts: Only when the body is a single statement
exp: No gate exists above a post-test body.
One full pass runs before the satisfied test releases control.

mcqs.q:
sum = 0, n = 5
REPEAT
  sum = sum + n
  n = n - 1
UNTIL n = 2
PRINT sum, n
exp: n lands on 2 exactly when the equality exits.

mcqs.q: REPEAT X = X + 1 UNTIL X >= 10 behaves like which C-language construct?
exp: Infosys asked this verbatim-flavoured identification item.
Body-first execution plus exit-on-true equals do-while(NOT C).

mcqs.q:
c = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT 'X'
  c = c + 1
UNTIL c > 3
How many times is X printed?
exp: Prints occur on passes with c = 1, 2, 3.
After the third print c becomes 4 and 4 > 3 exits.

mcqs.q: Which of these loops CAN execute ZERO times?
opts: All of them always run once
exp: Only pre-test loops can skip their body completely.
Both post-test forms guarantee at least one pass.

mcqs.q:
Integer i
Set i = 3
REPEAT
  PRINT i + 3
  i = i - 1
UNTIL i = 0
What is the output?
mcqs.source: Asked in Capgemini pseudo-code round (as do-while)
exp: Pass 1 prints 3+3 = 6, i becomes 2.
Pass 2 prints 5, i becomes 1. Pass 3 prints 4, i becomes 0.
Equality test now TRUE -> exit. Output 6 5 4.
mcqs.shortcut: Countdown by 1 from 3: exactly three passes; add 3 to each countdown value.

mcqs.q:
Integer i
Set i = 3
REPEAT
  PRINT i + 3
  i = i - 1
UNTIL i < 0
What is the output?
exp: Strict '< 0' needs i to reach -1.
Changing = to < adds a whole extra pass versus the i = 0 version.
mcqs.pattern: Boundary flip (= 0 vs < 0) shifts the exit row by exactly one pass here.

mcqs.q:
x = 1
REPEAT
  x = x + 3
UNTIL x >= 20
How many passes run?
exp: Formula: ceil((20 - 1)/3) = ceil(6.33) = 7.
Tail check: after 6 passes x = 19 (not enough); 7th pass makes 22 -> exit.

mcqs.q:
x = 2
REPEAT
  x = x * 3
UNTIL x > 30
PRINT x
exp: Tripling chain: 6, 18, 54.
54 > 30 exits; PRINT shows 54.

mcqs.q:
Which WHILE loop matches this REPEAT-UNTIL?
i = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 5
exp: Negate the exit test: NOT(i > 5) = i <= 5.
Keep the body identical and move the test above it.

mcqs.q: A REPEAT-UNTIL exits on (a > 5 AND b < 3). Its WHILE continuation condition is:
opts: NOT(a > 5 AND b < 3) with AND kept
exp: De Morgan: negate both atoms, swap AND to OR.
a > 5 -> a <= 5; b < 3 -> b >= 3; connector becomes OR.
mcqs.pattern: Distractor B keeps AND — the classic De Morgan drop.

mcqs.q:
a = 1, b = 10
REPEAT
  a = a + 2
  b = b - 3
UNTIL a >= b
PRINT a, b
exp: Pass 1: a=3, b=7 -> 3 >= 7 false.
Pass 2: a=5, b=4 -> 5 >= 4 true -> exit.

mcqs.q:
Inputs arrive in order: 4, 9, -1.
count = 0
REPEAT
  READ num
  count = count + 1
UNTIL num = -1
PRINT count
exp: Every read consumes one input and counts one pass.
The sentinel -1 IS read (that is how the test sees it): count = 3.
mcqs.pattern: Prompts = reads = passes; sentinel included in the count.

mcqs.q: Marks validation: REPEAT { OUTPUT "Enter marks"; INPUT mark } UNTIL mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100. Inputs tried: 150, then 55. How many prompts appear?
exp: Pass 1 reads 150 -> outside range -> repeat.
Pass 2 reads 55 -> accepted -> exit. Two prompts total.

mcqs.q:
total = 0
FOR j = 1 TO 2
  k = 1
  REPEAT
    total = total + k
    k = k + 1
  UNTIL k > 3
ENDFOR
PRINT total
exp: Inner loop folds k = 1, 2, 3 -> adds 6 per outer pass.
FOR runs j = 1, 2 -> two inner cycles -> 12.

mcqs.q:
n = 5
REPEAT
  n = n - 2
UNTIL n <= 1
PRINT n
exp: Walk: 3 (fails <= 1), then 1 (passes) -> exit.
PRINT shows 1.

mcqs.q:
x = 10
REPEAT
  x = x + 1
UNTIL x = 5
What happens when this executes?
exp: First pass lifts x to 11 before any test exists.
Counting upward never revisits 5 -> endless.
mcqs.pattern: Equality target BEHIND the moving counter = infinite.

mcqs.q:
flag = FALSE
count = 0
REPEAT
  PRINT count
UNTIL flag = TRUE
Why does this loop forever?
opts: flag is never updated inside the body
exp: Sabotage check 1: the tested variable appears nowhere in the body.
Frozen test answer = endless repetition.
mcqs.pattern: 'Infinite loop' option + untouched test variable = pick infinite without tracing.

mcqs.q:
num = 47, rev = 0
REPEAT
  d = num MOD 10
  rev = rev * 10 + d
  num = num DIV 10
UNTIL num = 0
PRINT rev
exp: Pass 1: d=7, rev=7, num=4. Pass 2: d=4, rev=74, num=0 -> exit.
Digits reversed: 74.
mcqs.shortcut: rev = rev*10 + digit is the universal reverse-number pipeline.

mcqs.q:
a = 12, b = 8
REPEAT
  IF a > b THEN a = a - b ELSE b = b - a ENDIF
UNTIL a = b
PRINT a
exp: Pass 1: a>b so a = 4; test fails.
Pass 2: b>a so b = 4; equality exits.
This subtraction-GCD yields gcd(12,8) = 4.
mcqs.pattern: Subtraction-GCD skeleton terminates exactly at the GCD.

mcqs.q:
t = 0
REPEAT
  t = t + 5
UNTIL t = 20
How many passes run?
exp: Equality lands exactly on pass four.

mcqs.q:
x = 1
REPEAT
  x = x + 1
UNTIL NOT(x < 5)
PRINT x
exp: x walks 2, 3, 4, 5; at 5 the negated test turns TRUE -> exit.
mcqs.pattern: NOT(...) wrappers are just De Morgan in disguise — unwrap first.

mcqs.q:
res = 5
REPEAT
  res = res - 1
  res = res + 1
UNTIL res = 0
What happens?
opts: Infinite loop because res never changes net
exp: Each pass cancels itself: -1 then +1 leaves res at 5.
Test value frozen -> endless repetition.
mcqs.pattern: Scan bodies for paired opposite updates whenever 'infinite' is an option.

mcqs.q:
i = 2
REPEAT
  PRINT i * i
  i = i + 2
UNTIL i > 6
Output?
exp: Squares printed: 4 (i=2), 16 (i=4), 36 (i=6).
i reaches 8 -> exit; 64 never prints.

mcqs.q: To display a menu AT LEAST ONCE and re-display it after every invalid choice, the best construct is:
exp: Menus must render before any choice exists -> post-test requirement.
WHILE would need artificial priming input.

mcqs.q:
x = 0
REPEAT
  PRINT x
UNTIL x > 0
What happens?
exp: Pass 1 prints 0; test 0 > 0 false.
x never changes, so every later test fails identically -> endless zeros.
Subtle trap: the condition LOOKS satisfiable, but nothing inside drives it.
mcqs.pattern: Looks-reachable target + no update = still infinite.

mcqs.q:
p = 1, i = 1
REPEAT
  p = p * i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 4
PRINT p
exp: Folds i = 1, 2, 3, 4 into p.
p = 4! = 24; i reaches 5 -> exit.
mcqs.shortcut: Factorial skeleton inside REPEAT: same folding, test moved below.

mcqs.q:
i = 5. Consider:
(A) WHILE i <= 3 { PRINT i; i = i + 1 }
(B) REPEAT { PRINT i; i = i + 1 } UNTIL i > 3
What does (B) do?
exp: (A) skips entirely — entry violates its condition.
(B) burns one guaranteed pass printing 5, then i = 6 > 3 exits.
Exactly the behavioural gap between pre-test and post-test.
mcqs.pattern: Violated-entry comparisons: WHILE 0 passes vs REPEAT 1 pass.

mcqs.q:
n = 29, s = 0
REPEAT
  s = s + n MOD 10
  n = n DIV 10
UNTIL n = 0
PRINT s
exp: Digits harvested: 9 then 2.
Digit sum of 29 = 11.
mcqs.pattern: Same digit-sum skeleton as WHILE questions; only the test position changed.

mcqs.q: For REPEAT v = v + s UNTIL v >= T with start a (a < T, s > 0), the number of passes is:
exp: Need smallest k with a + k*s >= T.
Solve: k >= (T-a)/s -> ceiling.
mcqs.shortcut: Floor+1 belongs to strict '>' exits; ceiling belongs to '>=' exits.

mcqs.q:
x = 1, y = 0
REPEAT
  IF x MOD 2 = 0 THEN y = y + x ELSE y = y - x ENDIF
  x = x + 1
UNTIL x > 5
PRINT y
exp: Signs follow parity: -1 +2 -3 +4 -5.
x reaches 6 -> exit; PRINT -3.
mcqs.pattern: Alternating-sign series inside post-test loop: fold carefully, exit row included.

mcqs.q:
a = 40, b = 1
REPEAT
  a = a DIV 2
  b = b * 3
UNTIL a <= b
PRINT a, b
exp: Rows: (20,3) fail; (10,9) fail; (5,27) succeed.
Halving meets tripling at 5 and 27.

mcqs.q:
n = 100, c = 0
REPEAT
  n = n DIV 2
  c = c + 1
UNTIL n < 10
PRINT c, n
exp: 6 < 10 exits on the fourth halving.
mcqs.shortcut: Halving counts are log2 hops across the threshold.

mcqs.q:
valid = FALSE, tries = 0
REPEAT
  tries = tries + 1
UNTIL valid = TRUE OR tries = 3
The loop is guaranteed to stop when:
opts: tries reaches 3 or valid becomes TRUE — whichever happens first
exp: OR-ed exit fires on the FIRST satisfied atom.
Even if valid never flips, tries hits 3 and releases control.
mcqs.pattern: Safety-counter pattern: bounded retry loops always terminate.

mcqs.q:
s = 0, n = 1
REPEAT
  s = s + n
  n = n + 2
UNTIL s >= 9
PRINT s, n
exp: Odd numbers fold: 1 (s=1), 3 (s=4), 5 (s=9).
9 >= 9 exits; n has already advanced to 7.
mcqs.pattern: Exit tests the ACCUMULATOR, not the counter — track both columns separately.

mcqs.q:
r = 0, i = 1
REPEAT
  j = 1
  REPEAT
    r = r + 1
    j = j + 1
  UNTIL j > i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i > 3
PRINT r
exp: Outer i=1: inner runs once (r=1). Outer i=2: inner twice (r=3). Outer i=3: inner three times (r=6).
Triangle sum 1+2+3 = 6.
mcqs.pattern: Variable-bound nested REPEAT builds triangular counts.

mcqs.q:
i = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT i
  i = i + 1
UNTIL i = 6
PRINT i
Full output?
exp: Loop prints 1..5; exiting pass leaves i = 6.
Trailing PRINT outside the loop emits 6.
mcqs.pattern: Separate loop-internal prints from the after-loop print — counters overshoot by design.

mcqs.q: REPEAT body UNTIL (x = 0 OR y = 0). The equivalent WHILE continuation condition is:
exp: Negate the OR: both atoms flip and OR becomes AND.
Continue only while BOTH variables are nonzero.
mcqs.pattern: De Morgan on OR-exits produces AND continuations — the swap direction most candidates forget.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a loop available in the C language?
exp: C provides exactly three loops: for, while, do-while.
repeat-until is Pascal/Cambridge pseudocode vocabulary; C expresses it as do-while(!cond).
mcqs.pattern: Vocabulary-origin questions reward knowing WHICH family each keyword belongs to.

mcqs.q:
x = 1
REPEAT
  PRINT x
  x = x + 2
UNTIL x = 8
What happens?
opts: Infinite loop — x skips over 8 with odd steps
exp: x visits odd numbers only: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 …
Equality with 8 is never met -> endless odd outputs.
(8 - 1) mod 2 = 1 flags the miss instantly.
mcqs.shortcut: Divisibility pre-check: (target - start) mod step != 0 predicts infinite BEFORE tracing.

mcqs.q:
a = 7, out = ""
REPEAT
  IF a MOD 2 = 0 THEN out = "0" + out ELSE out = "1" + out ENDIF
  a = a DIV 2
UNTIL a = 0
PRINT out
exp: Parity bits of 7 harvested LSB-first: 1, 1, 1.
Prepending reverses them into reading order: "111" = binary 7.
a starves to 0 after three DIV halvings -> exit.
mcqs.pattern: Prepend-vs-append decides bit order in binary-conversion skeletons.
